newsitem.title: FINLAND: Analysts see lower Finnair H1, want cuts.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see lower Finnair H1, want cuts.

text.p: Finnish national carrier Finnair Oy is expected to post clearly lower first-half profits on Friday due to higher wage costs and surging jet fuel prices, analysts said.
They said there were hopes that Finnair would find a way to follow the example set by other airlines such as Scandinavian airline SAS and unveil cost-cutting plans to boost profitability.
"There are expectations that Finnair will announce savings measures, as its competitors have done, in the near future," said analyst Tanja Lounevirta at Merita Bank.
"I would prefer to see announcements together with the six-month report," she added.

Finnair's financial year runs from April to March and the median of analysts' forecasts for its April-September profit after financial items is 292 million markka, down from 463 million in the year-ago period.
"Now would be a good time to squeeze costs and one way to do it could be through wage costs," said a transportation analyst at a Swedish bank, speaking on condition of anonymity.
He estimated that this year alone Finnair's wage costs would rise five percent.
But Finnair has already lightened its cost burden and some analysts said there was not much left to do.
"Finnair already made wide cost saving measures in the early part of the 1990s when payrolls were reduced and wages were frozen," said Aktia Bank's Ritva Ojala.
"I don't think they can afford to cut down personnel any more."

The effect of high fuel prices on profits was not Finnair's main problem in the long run, said Opstock analyst Rami Kinnala, adding that a 40 percent rise in jet fuel prices had increased costs by only 1-2 percent.
"And that is something Finnair can almost cover by raising fares," Kinnala said.
Finnair said on Tuesday it would raise ticket fares to Europe by two percent and to the U.S. by three percent on December 15, as proposed by the International Air Transport Association (IATA).
IATA proposed a global three percent hike in fares in response to the rise in fuel prices this year.
More of a problem for Finnair is that it stands to lose its sheltered position on Finnish routes as international competitors are eyeing the market.
SAS for one had expressed interest in the domestic routes, analysts said.
"Finland would be a natural extension to SAS's already dominant position in the Nordics," said Kinnala.
